The bilateral filter operates by mixing nearby source pixels according to both their spatial distance and color similarity. The color similarity can be computed from the optional guide input. Input: Set the left and right views, and choose a 'Latlong' projection to calculate disparity with spherical continuity.Vector Generation: Control the detail and matching in the disparity calculation. C_GenerateMap 2.1v5: Allows you to create an identity stmap in UV domain or an identity ppass map in XYZ latlong domain. The UV channels represent the absolute pixel positions of an image normalised between 0 and 1, whereas the XYZ channels represent the normalised 3D coordinates of a latlong image ranging between -1 and 1. If the Map parameter is set to ppass, then XYZ data will be written to the first three channels of the selected layer. If the Map parameter is set to stmap, then UV data will be written to the first two channels. All remaining channels (if any) will be set to zero. The Source input is optional: if present the format of Source will determine the format of the output map and Source will be also passed-through in the rgba layer. If no Source is given, the format of the output map will be defined by the Format parameter.

C_GlobalWarp 2.1v5: Analyse and correct input footage from a rig using the camera metadata to minimise the ghosting in the overlapping regions. The correction is based on the camera matches, which are used to find the best grid warp transformation of each input footage at the given convergence depth. Keying: Set analysis keys where there is structure and/or a depth change in the overlap region between images. Analysis: Control the warping process. Analyse the sequence to find the camera matches at the analysis keys, and then warp to align the input footage. You can add new keys anytime, and compute the camera matches at those keys only. Settings: Control the parameters underpinning the warping process. Line Constraints: Constraints can be added to keep lines straight during the warping. Create as many line constraints as needed. Add the constraint keys to the analysis keys. Optionally compute camera matches at the new keys. Finally update the warp. Output: The stitched panorama is shown in the main view. Set the output format, blend type, and resampling filter to render the final panorama. Each camera view will show the input footages. If the camera views are unwarped a stitch map layer will also be provided.

nodes.description: C_Stitcher 2.1v5: Stitch camera images to produce a seamless panorama. Input: Set the projection type for the input views. C_STMap 2.1v5: Allows you to warp the src image according to the stmap or ppass map. An stmap has two channels U and V representing the absolute positions of the source pixels normalised between 0 and 1, where (0,0) is the bottom left corner of the input image, and (1,1) is the top right corner. A ppass has three channels X, Y, and Z representing the normalised 3D coordinates of the source image in latlong domain.

Cryptomatte: Generates a matte that allows modification of parts of a 3D scene in a 2D render. To use, place the node on a stream that contains Cryptomatte layers (e.g. provided by an exr file, with Cryptomatte AOVs included). Then tick the Picker Add knob and use Ctrl+click or Ctrl+Shift+drag to select ID mattes from the viewer. These are then used to generate a matte in the target channel, specified by the Matte Output knob. Once an ID matte is selected, its name gets added to the Matte List knob. Similarly to Picker Add, you can use the Picker Remove knob to remove selected ID mattes. You can also manipulate selected ID mattes by modifying the text in Matte List. The Cryptomatte specifications were created at Psyop by Jonah Friedman and Andy Jones. They define a fully automatic method for creating and encoding ID mattes. 3D scenes consist of an organised hierarchy of objects and relationships, and when 2D images are rendered, that information is not preserved. ID mattes attempt to preserve organisational information by establishing a correspondence between items in the 3D scene and particular pixels in the 2D image plane.

Denoise: Uses spatial or temporal filtering to remove noise or grain without losing image quality. Motion Input: An optional input for attaching pre-calculated motion vectors, such as those created by VectorGenerator. Denoise can generate motion vectors internally, but connecting this input may produce significantly faster results. Temporal Processing: When enabled, uses frames on both sides of the current frame to perform temporal frame blending, which may produce a better denoise result. The number of frames used on either side of the current frame is determined by the Temporal Frame Offset control. When disabled, uses only the current frame to produce the denoise result. Frame Blending: Sets the variance allowed between regions in blended frames. Higher values attempt to blend more regions, but can lose image detail. This control is only available when Temporal Processing is enabled. Temporal Frame Offset: Sets the number of frames, on either side of the current frame, used to calculate the denoise effect.This control is only available when Temporal Processing is enabled. Lift Blacks: When enabled, blacks in the image are lifted toward white. This can be particularly useful if your image contains a lot of sub-blacks, areas of black with a value less than 0. Preserve Edges: When enabled, Denoise attempts to sharpen the image at edges to prevent over-smoothing, though this can emphasize noise in some cases.

nodes.description: The DiskCache node caches all the lines that pass through it to disk at full 32 bit floating point. You can speed up working with a complicated project by putting DiskCache nodes at strategic expensive points in your comp so that everything downstream uses the cached lines rather than requiring calculation of the upstream nodes. It is important to understand that DiskCache writes to disk only the lines it sees. Therefor the entire image may not be cached -- only the lines that were required and rendered. For instance if you are working in the GUI with the viewer image zoomed down so not all lines are visible, the lines that aren't visible won't be rendered. Zooming in or applying an operation like Blur can require more lines around the ones already computed and cached and will force the nodes above the DiskCache to execute to compute them. To force all lines in the frame to be calculated and cached, run the Precache. The cache location can be set in your Preferences' disk cache option. A large, fast local disk is DiskCache's best friend.

DisplaceGeo is a modifier that moves each vertex in the input geometry by the pixel value that corresponds with it in the input image. The geometry's UV map is used to sample the pixel value to use at each vertex.There are several ways you can displace the input geometry based on the image. The simplest is to use a single channel to drive a displacement along the vertices' normals. For this, choose luminance, red, green, or blue as the source. You can also use three channels. In this case, you can select rgb absolute to move the vertices to absolute positions defined by the pixel values if the channels are XYZ render pass, or select rgb relative to offset the existing vertex XYZ positions by the values of the three channels of image input.

nodes.description: Erode blurs and then scales and clamps the output pixels such that a solid black & white matte is enlarged or shrunk by a given amount. The channel blurred with a triangle filter of twice the size s, which turns a sharp 0-1 transition into a quadratic. A slope is then chosen so a point at size+.5 away from the sharp transition turns into zero and a point at size-.5 away turns into a one. Notice that solid areas of any color other than 0 or 1 will change their color, as they are treated as the antialiased edge. This can only be corrected by doing a different algorithm where a min or max of an area is done rather than this blur operation, see FilterErode for a slow implementation.
Box Morphological Filter Maximum (or minimum) of a rectangular area around each pixel. This can be used to grow or shrink mattes.

Morphological Filter For each output pixel, the input pixels are multiplied by the coefficients of a blurring filter, and then the maximum of the results is taken (if the size argument is negative). This will cause brighter areas to grow into darker areas. For positive arguments the filter is multiplied by 1-pixel and 1-maximum is returned. This will cause darker areas to grow into lighter areas.

Multiplies the image by a constant, selected using Exposure terminology. This can also add a constant to Cineon data that has been read raw from the file such that log2lin will produce a similar result.

To reference pixels in other channels, use layer.channel, for example, matte.garbage. If the layer name is not present, the channel is assumed to be in the current layer. As a shortcut, the rgba layer's red, green, blue, and alpha can be referenced as r, g, b, and a.

F_Align 4.6v4.539224 F_Align uses Global Motion Estimation (GME) to calculate a four corner pin so that each frame in one shot will be aligned with the corresponding frame in a second reference shot. Help->Documentation contains a more detailed description of this plug-in. Copyright 2026 The Foundry all rights reserved.

F_DeFlicker2 4.6v4.539224 F_DeFlicker2 is used to get rid of two types of flicker from a shot, in-scene and archive. In-Scene flicker is localised, for example from an unsynchronised fluorescent light, and dependent on the geometry of the scene. Archive flicker is smoothly, spatially varying flicker, such as that from an old black and white film. See also F_DeFlicker1 in the full Furnace suite. Help->Documentation contains a more detailed description of this plug-in. Copyright 2026 The Foundry all rights reserved.

F_ReGrain 4.6v4.539224 F_ReGrain is used to add grain to a sequence. It can either replicate the grain from the 'Grain' input, or apply stock grain. The response of grain to luminance can also be sampled from the 'Grain' input. Each press of the 'Analyse Response' button will add samples to the the response curve. This curve can be tweaked with several parameters. Help->Documentation contains a more detailed description of this plug-in. Copyright 2026 The Foundry all rights reserved.

F_RigRemoval 4.6v4.539224 F_RigRemoval is used to remove foreground items from a scene, using inter-frame motion to guess at a reconstruction for the missing data behind the foreground object. The foreground region has to be masked through the whole sequence, either with a white shape in the Mask sequence, using the box region or using the alpha channel. Red regions indicate areas which haven't (or can't) be reconstructed. It may be necessary to increase Frames Used to include more frames before the repair can be completed. RigRemoval performs best where the background behind the foreground object is 'static'; that is - apart from DVE-style moves it doesn't vary much from frame to frame. Help->Documentation contains a more detailed description of this plug-in. Copyright 2026 The Foundry all rights reserved.

F_Steadiness 4.6v4.539224 F_Steadiness calculates a four corner pin on a clip so that all frames in a clip are locked to a single frame or the pin is calculated by smoothing out a window of motion about the current frame. F_Steadiness will not work properly if used on a render farm with 'Incremental Lock' turned on and must instead be processed locally. Help->Documentation contains a more detailed description of this plug-in. Copyright 2026 The Foundry all rights reserved.

F_WireRemoval 4.6v4.539224 Many effects movies feature complicated stunts that require an actor to be suspended by wires for their safety. These wires need to be digitally removed. There are many ways of doing this including painting the wires out frame by frame and replacing large parts of the background to cover the wires. The method used depends on the type of image under the wire. Furnace is particularly good at replacing the painting method but it also includes tools to assist in clean plating when new backgrouinds have to be tracked into place. F_WireRemoval is particularly good at removing wires over heavily motion blurred backgrounds or wires over smoke, dust or clouds. It can be used to remove each wire in a sequence or to quickly create a clean plate which can then be tracked into place. Help->Documentation contains a more detailed description of this plug-in. Generates a 3D Field
FieldCrop: Crops an input field to a bounding box.

FieldImage: Makes a 3D field from a 2D image. If no camera is connected, the image is placed on the XY plane in the unit square and extends along the Z axis to infinity. If a camera is connected, the image is instead projected through the camera frustum.
FieldInvert: Inverts a field. For a signed distance field, this means negating it do that the inside and outside become swapped. For other fields, it means subtracting from 1.
FieldMath Performs various maths operation on the inputs.

FieldMerge: Merges fields together. Operations are: Add Subtract Multiply Divide Minimum Maximum The following operations apply only to signed distance fields: Shape Union: Makes the union of shapes. Shape Intersection: Makes the intersection of shapes. Shape Subtraction: Subtracts shapes. Shape Exclusion: Makes the exclusion of shapes.
FieldMix: Interpolates between two fields according to a third field.
FieldPosition: Returns the input point unchanged. This is often useful in conjuction with FieldMath.
FieldRamp: Produces a field between two points which goes linearly from zero at the start point to one at the end point.

FieldShape: Creates a variety of simple shapes. Shapes can be described as signed distance fields or as density fields. Signed distance fields are generally more useful and can be converted to density fields later on using the FieldShapeToDensity node.

FieldShapeModify: Modifies a signed distance field. Operations are: Invert: Inverts a shape so the inside becomes the outside. Round: Adds a rounded edge. Shell: Turns a solid shape into a thin shell. Elongate: Lenthens a shape along an axis. Twist: Twists a shape. Bend: Bends a shape. Repeat: Repeats a shape through space. Limited Repeat: Repeats a shape through space a limited number of times. Repeat Polar: Repeats a shape around an axis. Mirror: Mirrors a shape about one or more axes. Extrude2D: Extrudes a 2D shape into a 3D shape. Revolve2D: Revolves a 2D shape into a 3D shape.

FieldShapeToDensity: Converts a signed distance field into a density field. Signed distance fields specify a sharp-edged surface, while density fields can be fuzzy. Downstream nodes which have mask inputs can generally deal with either type of field. The resulting field has a value of 1 inside the shape and zero outside with an optional fuzzy-edge ramp defined by the feather knob.

FieldTransform: Transforms the input field. If no input, then it transforms the current point. If the input field is a signed distance field, the distance will be adjusted by the uniform scaling factor to keep the field valid. Non-uniform scaling or skewing does not work with signed distance fields. A warning will be shown if you attempt this.

This shader puts a constant color into the selected channels, typically for the purpose of rendering a hold out using the affected geometry. This is essentially the same as using a Constant as the input texture but doesn't break the shading sequence so it works properly when applied after other Material operators. Set the channels to rgb to affect just the color channels or rgba to also knock out the alpha.

Nuke supports Lens Flares by providing three different rendering operators: flares, sparkles and reflections. This operator creates flares that can be combined to create film or video camera lens flares. Flares are created by reflections between lenses in the multilayer lens setup inside a camera. Flares are generally round, oval, or roundish with 5 or 6 flattened sides. Due to different reflection and refraction coefficients based on wavelength, flares tend to show chroma shifting, generating rainbow-like outlines. Nuke Flares are implemented as a donut-like shape with a possibly filled center. Mmmm... donuts.... There are three radii: the outer radius is the outside of the donut, the middle radius is the thickest part, and the inner radius is where the donut hole would be. A flare defines two colors, the color of the donut itself, and the fill color for the donut 'hole'. If donut color and hole color are the same, flares will be rendered as disks.

The GridWarp3 node enables the user to warp an input image via the use of spline lines in the form of a 2D grid. Control points and their tangents can be moved, animated and linked to trackers. The input is distorted according to the output type selected and the topology of the source and destination grids. Both warping and morphing can be accomplished with this node by keying warp and mix parameters. If there is no destination image provided, then the mix and warp parameters are ignored. The output is produced by warping images between the source and destination grids by the warp amount and mixing the warped source and destination images by the mix amount. The source image is warped from the source positions towards the destination positions by the warp amount (0 to 1 equals 0 to 100%). The destination image (if supplied) is warped from the destination positions towards the source positions by 1-warp. The results are then mixed based on the mix parameter (0 = source, 1 = destination, .5 = 50% of each).

The LiveGroup node behaves similar to a Precomp node which contains its own subgraph and nodes, but behaves differently in that the contents may be published to an external nuke script. This can be used to break down large workflows into smaller, more manageable scripts which are then distributed out to artists for greater collaboration. Once a LiveGroup is published, the contents become locked which prevents any modifications to the subgraph. Exceptions to this are the Viewer node which can still be created and attached as normal, and knobs exposed on the LiveGroup nodes panel. When the LiveGroup node is editable, exposed knobs can be created by dragging and dropping knobs from the nodes within the subgraph, onto the LiveGroup node's panel, by using the Manage User knobs dialog or through the Python API with nuke.Link_Knob and setting the link to a knob inside the subgraph. Exposed knobs are also visible when the LiveGroup is opened in a separate Nuke session under the project settings panel. When the LiveGroup node is published with an exposed knob and the value of this knob changes, the exposed knob becomes an override knob. Override knobs are indicated by a yellow square in the node panel. When there are multiple knobs on a row, an overlapping icon is displayed which may be clicked to view the state of each of the knobs individually. Reloading the LiveGroup node will revert all changes made to the LiveGroup nodes contents, except for any override knobs, returning the LiveGroup to the state of the saved script. Using the context menu of an overriden knob, it is possible to revert individual overrides to the LiveGroup scripts value or (when editable) apply them to the LiveGroup script. The LiveGroup node also offers several Python callbacks which may be added to the node using node.addCallback: nuke.LIVEGROUP_CALLBACK_CAN_PUBLISH Executes before publishing when the contents are still editable, and prevents the action if the callback returns Falsenuke.LIVEGROUP_CALLBACK_PUBLISHED Executes after a successful publish action when the contents are lockednuke.LIVEGROUP_CALLBACK_CAN_MAKE_EDITABLE Executes before the LiveGroup is made editable when the contents are still locked, and prevents the action if the callback returns Falsenuke.LIVEGROUP_CALLBACK_MADE_EDITABLE Executes after the LiveGroup is made editable, when the contents are made editablenuke.LIVEGROUP_CALLBACK_RELOADED Executes when the LiveGroup has been reloadednuke.PRECOMP_CALLBACK_OPENED Executes when the LiveGroup has been opened in a separate Nuke session See also: LiveInput node.

The LiveInput is a type of Input node. Adding a LiveInput to a container type node, such as a Group, Precomp or LiveGroup will add a corresponding input connection to that container node. LiveInput nodes are intended to be used in conjunction with LiveGroup nodes so that artists working on LiveGroup scripts can work on the script in the context of a parent script without the need for rendering. When a LiveInput is parented to a LiveGroup Node (i.e. when viewing a LiveGroup structure from within a parent session) it will act like a simple Input. It will just pipe through whatever is connected to the corresponding input for the parent LiveGroup Node. When a LiveInput is part of a LiveGroup script which is opened in its own session, it will act as a container node where the contents are read from the corresponding input of the LiveGroup defined by the liveGroup knob in the nuke script defined by the file knob. The input can be Reloaded using the Reload button.

MatchGrade Use MatchGrade to automatically calculate a grade to match source to target footage. Match Graded Source: MatchGrade can be used to extract a baked-in grade by matching the source footage with a graded version of the source. Use this to create and export the grade to use with the original source footage. The same frames are expected on the source and target inputs and the source and target pixels need to be aligned. Press 'Auto Align Target to Source' to automatically compute the alignment. Match Different Clip: MatchGrade can also be used to match the grade in a different clip where the source and target frames are different. Use this to create a grade to reproduce the look of the target in the source footage. You can for example create the grade to match an element between different shots by using the mask input to match the colors on the element only in the different clips. Analyze Reference Frames: The grade is calculated by analysing a set of reference frames. First set the matching task then key reference frames that pick out the characteristic colors in each sequence. Finally, press 'Analyze Reference Frames' to calculate the grade. Export: The grade can be exported in .csp format for use with the OCIO FileTransform node. A CDL transform can also be calculated and exported to OCIO CDLTransform. There is the option to manually set CDL parameters and recalculate the best fit transform. Auto-analyze Per Frame: You can calculate the best grade to use on a frame-by-frame basis when extracting a baked in grade. Select 'Auto-analyze per frame' when the task is set to 'Match Graded Source' to enable this.

ModelBuilder Use the ModelBuilder to create a 3D model for a shot given a tracked camera. You can build a model by creating shapes then editing them; and you can align models over your shot footage by dragging vertices to their corresponding 2D location. Create: Use the left-hand toolbar to create a Point, Card, Cube, Sphere, Cone or Cylinder shape. You can set default values for creating new shapes such as distance and tessellation. When you create a new shape it will be added to the scene graph tree in the properties panel. You can use the scene-graph to name, order, group and set the visibility for shapes. Create a new group using the '+' button, then drag and drop to create a hierarchy. Align: Align mode calculates a 3D position for an object that matches its position in the source footage as closely as possible without distorting the shape. To use it you must have an input camera and the viewer must be locked to it; this will happen automatically whenever you switch into Align mode. Position shapes by dragging several of their vertices over their correct 2D locations; then change to a different frame and repeat the process. It should only be necessary to do this for 4 or 5 of the vertices for each object. When you've placed a vertex on one frame, a guideline will be shown on other frames to indicate where the correct location might be. Edit: Starting with one of the primitive shapes, you can perform various editing operations to sculpt it into the shape you desire. Editing operations include moving, scaling, carving, extruding and bevelling. Operations apply to the currently selected vertices, edges, faces or shapes and are found on the viewer's right-click menu. Press Enter to accept the results of an operation or Escape to cancel it. Tips: You can use input geometry as a reference while modelling. Select vertices on the input geo before creating a shape and the created shape will be fitted to the vertices automatically. The PointCloudGenerator is especially handy for this. You can hold down Shift to place a new shape on the surface of some existing geometry. If you keep Shift held down while you move the cursor, the yellow circle will change orientation to match the geometry underneath the cursor. Carving has to start on an existing edge or vertex; subsequent clicks must be inside the highlighted area. You can do freehand carving by holding down Ctrl+Shift while you drag the mouse.

Existing shapes and paint strokes can be edited in the node control panel by selecting an item (or items) from the list or in the Viewer. Click on a toolbar item to cycle through the available options for that class of tools. Click and hold or right-click on a toolbar button to open that submenu and select any of its available tool types. Roto ShapesCreationTo create a roto shape, select a spline tool and click in the Viewer to place points. You can drag while clicked down to pull out Bezier handles or adjust B-Spline tension as you create the shape. To finish creating the shape and close it, click on the first point or press the enter key. To finish but leave the shape open, press the ESC key. Soft EdgeTo pull out the soft edge, drag on the small line perpendicular to the spline at that point or Ctrl+drag from the point. If the 'feather lock' option is set, dragging on a control point will move both it and its corresponding soft edge point, otherwise they move independently. Ctrl+drag on a main edge point to temporarily invert the current 'feather link' setting. Press 'E' to increase the feather point distance on the selected points. Press Shift+'E' to reset the selected points' feather points to the main point positions. BezierShift+drag on a tangent handle to snap the opposite handle to the same length. Ctrl+drag on a tangent handle to move it independently of its opposite handle. B-SplineShift+Ctrl+drag on a point to adjust its tension.The tension is weighted with a power function of 4. PaintShift+click and drag to set the brush size. Clone OffsetCtrl+click and drag to adjust the clone source offset relative to its current position. Ctrl+Shift+click and drag to reset the clone source offset. Clone SourceSelect the Background as source to clone from the primary input. Select Foreground to clone from the currently accumulated result. Note that cloning from the Foreground can cause slower renders. In this case, the order each stroke is rendered matters, so strokes must be rendered sequentially and rendering can't be optimized as it can be when cloning directly from an input image. Press the 'T' key to toggle visibility of the source onion-skin overlay and source transform handles. All SplinesCtrl+Alt+click on the spline to add a point. Press 'Z' to increase smoothness at a point and Shift+'Z' to cusp it. Press the Delete key to delete a point. Transform Jack/BoxCtrl+drag on an edge to skew. Ctrl+drag on the center point to move it independent of the selection. Ctrl+rotate to rotate the jack without moving points. Shift+drag on the jack or box will disable snapping.

The SplineWarp node enables the user to generate arbitrary warpings of an input image through the use of pins and roto splines. Either can be placed in the frame to define source and destination regions. Any curve can also be marked as a boundary to prevent warping outside of the defined area. Correspondence points can be created along the splines. These points pair up locations on the A and B splines to provide control over how the image is warped. They can also be used to increase warping accuracy in selected areas since each segment is subdivided by the curve resolution. The curves panel presents a hierarchical stack/list interface of the curves and pins for managing the warp effect. Both warping and morphing can be accomplished with this node by keying warp and mix parameters. If there is no B image provided, then the mix parameter is ignored. The output is produced by warping images between the A and B markers by the warp amount and mixing the warped A and B images by the mix amount. The A image is warped from the A positions towards the B positions by the warp amount (0 to 1 equals 0 to 100%). The B image (if supplied) is warped from the B positions towards the A positions by 1-warp. The results are then mixed based on the mix parameter (0 = A, 1 = B, .5 = 50% of each). NOTE: At the moment only the first hard boundary curve affects the warp, other hard boundary curves are ignored! Hard boundary curves most also be closed.

Ultimatte AdvantEdge technology is the culmination of over 25 years of bluescreen imaging experience by Ultimatte Corporation. While individual controls for the keying parameters are accessable for fine tuning, most keys can be set up using the interactive picking tools in the Viewer toolbar. The image is analyzed and Ultimatte AdvantEdge automatically calculates optimum settings for several different parameters simultaneously. This powerful analysis allows Ultimatte AdvantEdge to offer a very simple user interface without sacrificing flexibility and image control. The final result is a composite that preserves fine details like hair, smoke, and motion blurred edges with a minimum of compromises. In most cases you will use the Viewer toolbar pickers in order from left to right. First pick the screen color from a representative backing area near detail that you want to retain. Next, activate the overlay display and use the overlay + and - pickers to get the overlay to cover as much of the screen as possible without intruding on the foreground subject area. The overlay indicates areas that will definitely not be in the composite. Now turn the overlay view off, view the alpha channel, and use the matte + and - pickers to bring areas more solidly into the matte or remove noise or other aberrations from the matte. The Hold Shadow tool can also be used to indicate shadows that should be retained in the final composite, rather than using the matte + tool to bring them into the matte. This allows the shadows to be handled separately (and more accurately) from foreground subject areas. Finally, you can use the spill and match pickers to improve the color correction applied to the RGB channels.
